newsitem.title: USA: Sun targets revenues, aggressive pricing. [CORRECTED 02:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sun targets revenues, aggressive pricing. [CORRECTED 02:20 GMT]

text.p: Sun Microsystems Inc Chief Financial Officer Michael Lehman said the company is targeting revenue growth as it enters its fiscal 1998 to expand its growing influence as a computer systems supplier.

Lehman told analysts in a conference call the company's fourth quarter operating income reached a record 13.3 percent of revenues, as the company's net bookings rose 22.9 percent sequentially to $2.5 billion.
Lehman said the company "may have an increased appetite" for cash during the upcoming year, and may go to the market during the period to augment its cash postion.

The Sun Micrososystems CFO said Sun's book-to-bill ratio in its fiscal fourth quarter was 1-to-1, meaning that it received roughly $100 of new orders for every $100 worth of orders shipped. Its backlog was nearly $380 million, down a bit sequentially. (Corrects book-to-bill)
Lehman said the company added more than 800 people in the fourth quarter and expects to accelerate hiring early in the new fiscal year in areas that will boost revenue growth.

"Our business model has never been stronger," he said, adding the company plans to price its products aggressively as part of its plan to continue transforming the company into one of the corporate world's top suppliers of computing systems.

Lehman said the company saw no dramatic shift in the mix of its business, and that gross margins were 50.4 percent in the fourth quarter, but he said Sun continues to project this to decrease for its business planning purposes.
"We plan for lower gross margins going forward," he said.
Lehman said the company shipped a record number of systems in its fourth quarter, when revenues surged to a record $2.54 billion and net income hit $237.2 million, or $0.61 a share.
The earnings per share figure was above Wall Street's First Call consensus of $0.59. In fiscal fourth quarter 1996, per share earnings were $0.31, after a $0.12 one time charge.

Lehman said Sun, which is expanding offices in the Boston, Denver and San Francisco Bay areas, expects to increase the ratio of owned versus leased space, adding that real estate spending could double in fiscal 1998 to $300 million to $350 million.

Ed Zander, president of Sun's Sun Microsystems Computer Company, said server revenues had more than doubled year over year in the June quarter. The company usually does not break out its financial results by business sector.

Sun Chief Executive Scott McNealy said Sun would continue to look for "small, opportunistic acquisitions," but said there was no defined strategy to seek out acquisitions. Before the company's fourth quarter earnings were released Sun announced it had entered into a definitive agreement to acquire the assets of Encore Computer Corp's storage business at a purchase price of $185 million.

Lehman said Sun expects to continue to be cash generative and noted it ended the 1997 financial year with $1.1 billion in cash, but he said a need to raise funding on the market could arise, for example, if it made serveral acquisitions.
"We're going to spend a billion dollars in R&D over the next 12 months," McNealy said. In fiscal 1997, Sun spent nearly $826 million in research and development.

McNealy said Sun would soon elaborate on its product plans for offering its Solaris Unix operating system on computers equipped with processors compatible with Intel Corp microprocessors. Intel-compatible processors traditionally run with Microsoft Corp operating systems.
Lehman said the company aims to make its Solaris system accepted as the Unix platform of choice.
Zander said the company had sold more than $100 million of its new high-end Starfire servers in 100 days after launching the product.

The Sun executives made clear they aim to maintain their business model, but extend their profile to compete in major corporations head-to-head with Hewlett-Packard Co and International Business Machines Corp.

Lehman and McNealy said declining order backlog was partly a result of reducing the company's lead times for delivery products, and should not be considered an appropriate barometer of the strength of the company's future business.

In answer to questions from analysts and in a later telephone interview, Lehman said the company was not currently preparing to seek fresh financing, though it was not ruling out such a move in the coming year.
((-sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto, +1 415 846 5400)
